errors.problem: The tap gloss is looked up without the harakat/shadda, so on the minimal-pair pages the learner taps the second word and gets the gloss of the FIRST word or of an unrelated noun: كَاتَبَ (he corresponded with) shows 'writer' (= كَاتِب); دَرَّسَ (he taught) shows 'lesson' (= دَرْس) on three pages; جَمَال (beauty) shows 'camel (plural)' (plural of camel is جِمَال); حَجَزَ (he booked) shows 'booking, reservation' (= حَجْز); ظُهْر (noon) shows 'back (of the body)' (= ظَهْر). Each page exists to teach that these are different words, and the tap says they are the same.
errors.fix: Match tap glosses on the vocalised form (or add exact vocabulary entries): كَاتَبَ = he corresponded with; دَرَّسَ = he taught; جَمَال = beauty; حَجَزَ = he booked; ظُهْر = noon
errors.alsoChange: the .en fields of these pairs are already correct; only the tap lookup is wrong

errors.problem: هَال does not mean 'halo' (halo is هَالَة); هَال is cardamom (the spice). The pair itself is valid, only the gloss is wrong.
errors.alsoChange: pairs[0][1].en 'halo, cardamom' → 'cardamom'; tap gloss هَال=halo, cardamom → cardamom

errors.problem: ذَلِيل means lowly, abject, humiliated (a negative word); 'humble' (the virtue, مُتَوَاضِع) is misleading as the learner's only gloss

The Arabic is right but the engine transliterates a final yāʾ/wāw after ā as a second long vowel; the letter names are zāy and wāw (and the 'name' field says so), so the learner sees two different names for one letter
errors.fix: Zāy; Wāw (after ā a bare ي / و is the consonant y / w)

errors.problem: On the letter and pronunciation pages the single glyph ل is glossed as the preposition 'for; belonging to' and و as 'and' (the particles), while every other letter is glossed 'the letter …'; a beginner on the alphabet page learns that the letter lām means 'for'
errors.fix: ل=the letter lām; و=the letter wāw (prefer the letter entry when a bare glyph is tapped on a letters/pronunciation page)

notes.note: For ṣād the tip says 'pull the back of the tongue DOWN and back', while the emphatics page [3], ṭāʾ page [20] and ḍād page [17] say 'raise the back of the tongue up and back towards the soft palate'. Both describe real parts of the emphatic gesture (tongue-root retraction vs velarisation), but the learner meets two opposite instructions for the same sound; pick one wording for all four emphatics.

English anchors for the emphatic vowel differ: 'u in but' (emphatics), 'du of dull' (ḍād), 'sun or saw' (ṣād). The backed a after an emphatic is closer to the a of 'father' / o of 'hot' than to 'but'; not wrong enough to teach a wrong sound, but worth one consistent anchor.

ghayn is compared to the French r and placed 'near the uvula'. MSA ɣ is velar (the voiced partner of خ, as page [21] itself says); French r is uvular. Acceptable beginner approximation; the diagram of [21] (soft palate) is the accurate one.

notes.path: letters [6].example.ar خَيْر; letters [11].example.ar سَلَام; pronunciation [24].examples[1].ar السَّفَر; letters [24].example.ar نُور
notes.note: Tap glosses carry phrase-level remarks that do not fit the single word: خَيْر='goodness ("good night")', سَلَام='peace ("wow!" with yā)', السَّفَر='the travel ("passport")', نُور='Nour (first name)' where the page says 'light'. Not wrong, but confusing on an alphabet page.

The generated transliteration line of tips that contain bare diacritics or hamza seats drops them: 'The small w-shaped mark  (shadda)', 'sit on a seat: , i,  or .', '( i  )'. If the learner can see the ⟶ line for tips, these read as garbled; otherwise ignore.
The transliteration of the sun/moon diagram turns الشَّمْس into 'ash-shams → ash-shams', so the before/after contrast disappears in the ⟶ line (Arabic itself is right).
سَتَأْتِي is glossed only 'she will come'; it is equally 'you (m.) will come'. Fine for the page, but a learner who meets it in a dialogue addressed to a man may be confused.
IPA lists 'd͡ʒ | ʒ | g' (MSA plus two dialect values) while the letter entry gives only d͡ʒ. Intentional per the tip, but the letter page and the pronunciation page differ.
Tap gloss 'small cup' vs example.en 'cup' — same word, slightly different gloss; harmless.

summary: Checked all 31 letter entries (names, Arabic names, IPA, transliteration symbols, sun/moon status, sound descriptions, example words and glosses) and all 30 pronunciation pages (IPA, letters, tips, diagrams, common-error texts, examples and every minimal pair). Letter names, sun/moon assignments (14/14), IPA values and transliteration symbols are all correct; every minimal pair is a real pair with correct harakat and the .en glosses of the pairs are right. 5 errors: 2 major, 3 minor. The one systematic problem is the tap-gloss engine, which matches words without harakat/shadda, so on the minimal-pair pages the second word of the pair (كَاتَبَ, دَرَّسَ, جَمَال, حَجَزَ, ظُهْر) is glossed as the first word or an unrelated noun — exactly the confusion the pages are meant to remove. The only content error in the Arabic/English itself is هَال glossed 'halo' (it is cardamom), plus the mild 'humble' for ذَلِيل. Minor engine/gloss points: zāy/wāw transliterated Zāī/Wāū, and ل / و glossed as the particles 'for' / 'and' on the alphabet pages. Notes cover inconsistent tongue-position wording for the emphatics, English vowel anchors, the French-r comparison for ghayn, and garbled ⟶ lines where tips contain bare diacritics.
